OUTLINE VIEW

Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the history and clinical rationale for outpatient total joint arthroplasty.
Identify the unique considerations of outpatient total joint arthroplasty.
Understand and develop protocols for successful same-day discharge.
Identify risk factors for failure to meet the criteria for same-day discharge after total joint
arthroplasty.
Identify and understand how to prevent and manage complications associated with outpatient
joint arthroplasty.
History
Outpatient total joint replacement has been performed in the United States since the early
2000s.

Early studies began reporting outcomes in 2005 and showed promising results in specialized


History
Similar to many other surgical procedures, such as anterior cruciate ligament
reconstruction, fracture repair, and spine procedures, improvements in perioperative
care and surgical techniques have led to decreased hospital length of stay associated
with total joint arthroplasty. Although total joint arthroplasty was initially associated with
hospital length of stays of 5 days or longer, a steady downward trend has occurred in the
past 10 to 20 years, culminating in the current state of outpatient total joint arthroplasty,
defined by Medicare as a hospital length of stay of less than 24 hours or, more
commonly, defined by the International Association for Ambulatory Surgery as discharge
on the same day of the surgical procedure.
The earliest reports of outpatient arthroplasty in the United States were from Berger et
al1 in Chicago as early as 2005. Other early reports were from specialized centers with
complex postdischarge regimens that demonstrated positive outcomes with minimal
complications in a select group of patients.2 Other centers began reporting the results of
outpatient total joint arthroplasty in similarly select patients over the subsequent 10
years, and multiple small series were published during the next decade. In most studies,
few complications were reported to be specifically associated with early discharge in
appropriately selected patients.3,4
Clinical Rationale
Inpatient hospitalization after joint replacement was necessary because of pain and potential
for blood transfusion.
Modern pain protocols and blood management protocols can avoid the need for inpatient
hospitalization in carefully selected patients.


Clinical Rationale
As with many orthopaedic procedures, hospital length of stay for total joint arthroplasty
has decreased over time. Traditional inpatient hospital stays after total joint replacement
were most commonly necessary because of difficulty controlling the pain associated with
the procedure and the potential need for blood transfusion. Before the implementation
of current multimodal pain protocols, pain control after joint replacement was most
commonly achieved via patient-controlled analgesia with the use of parenteral narcotics.
These narcotics were associated with substantial adverse reactions, especially
gastrointestinal complications, including nausea, vomiting, and ileus, and caused
somnolence, which made participation in physical therapy difficult. Therefore, patients
required substantial time to achieve the physical therapy goals necessary for safe
discharge home, leading to prolonged hospital stays and a high rate of nonhome
discharge.
In addition, before the implementation of modern blood management techniques,
particularly tranexamic acid, the rate of transfusion after total joint arthroplasty was
reported to be as high as 38%.5 With a rate this high, it was necessary to closely monitor
postoperative laboratory values and be prepared to transfuse more than one-fourth of
patients. Therefore, inpatient hospital stays were necessary should transfusion be
necessary. Implementation of current blood management protocols have decreased the
transfusion rate to less than 1% in most studies; therefore, routine laboratory
monitoring and preparation for transfusion are no longer necessary in most patients.6,7
Considering improved pain control and a greatly reduced transfusion rate, inpatient
hospitalization after total joint arthroplasty is less necessary in a subset of patients.
Therefore, outpatient total joint arthroplasty can be considered if potential clinical or
societal benefits are achieved. The potential clinical and societal benefits are higher
levels of patient satisfaction, substantially decreased costs, and the potential for lower
infection rates.8-10
Outcomes of Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty

9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000019
3/20

Since 2005, many studies have been published on the outcomes of outpatient total joint
arthroplasty.
Most early studies were case series; however, since 2010, several large database studies and a
prospective randomized trial comparing inpatient versus outpatient total joint arthroplasty
have been performed, showing positive results for outpatient joint replacement.

Outcomes of Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty
The potential advantages of outpatient arthroplasty cannot be at the cost of a reduction
in outcomes associated with traditional inpatient arthroplasty. Therefore, much research
on outpatient arthroplasty has been focused on ensuring that outpatient arthroplasty is
as safe as inpatient arthroplasty.
In 2009, Kolisek et al2 compared inpatient versus outpatient total knee arthroplasty (TKA)
and found no short-term or midterm (mean follow-up, 2 years) differences between the
two groups regarding outcomes or complications. The authors concluded that outpatient
TKA in appropriately selected patients results in outcomes that are at least equivalent to
those of traditional inpatient TKA. In 2017, Springer et al11 reviewed the effect of
outpatient arthroplasty with regard to readmissions and unplanned episodes of care
and found no increase in either in patients who underwent outpatient total joint
arthroplasty. Nelson et al12 reviewed the National Surgical Quality Improvement
Program database and evaluated 63,844 total hip arthroplasty (THA) patients to compare
same-day discharge with an inpatient hospital stay. The authors found no difference in
any measured outcomes or complications between the two groups.12 In 2017, Courtney
et al13 also reviewed the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database and
evaluated THA and TKA patients and found that, in appropriately selected patients,
outpatient arthroplasty was associated with a decreased rate of complications compared
with inpatient total joint arthroplasty.13 In the 2017 Otto Aufranc Award–winning study,
Goyal et al14 performed a prospective, randomized trial of inpatient versus outpatient
THA and found no differences in revision surgery, readmission, emergency department
visits, acute office visits, or phone calls to the office postoperatively. Evaluating the

results of these studies and many other studies gives surgeons the confidence that, in
appropriately selected patients, outpatient arthroplasty is a safe option.
Preoperative Evaluation and Management
Patient Selection
Patient selection is the most important element of a successful and safe outpatient total joint
arthroplasty program.
Several resources are available to help define appropriate patient selection, including
comprehensive lists of absolute contraindications and the Outpatient Arthroplasty Risk
Assessment (OARA) score.

Patient Selection
Patient selection often is considered the most important element of successful
outpatient joint replacement. Several methods are available to evaluate a patient’s
appropriateness for outpatient discharge, the most comprehensive and well-studied of
which is the Outpatient Arthroplasty Risk Assessment score.15 Originally described by
Meneghini et al,15 this general medical questionnaire has been shown to be more
predictive than the American Society of Anesthesiologists classification or the Charlson
Comorbidity Index in determining a patient’s ability to safely and predictably undergo
outpatient total joint replacement. The Outpatient Arthroplasty Risk Assessment also
was independently validated in a different practice setting, adding to its strength as a
clinically useful tool.16 The six variables of the Outpatient Arthroplasty Risk Assessment
score most associated with an increased length of stay are summarized in Table 1.
Additional details on this system are found in Video 1.
Table 1 Variables of the Outpatient Arthroplasty Risk Assessment Score Associated With
Increased Hospital Length of Stay14
Diabetes mellitus: hemoglobin A1c level >7%

Others have attempted to determine patient selection by identifying specific
comorbidities associated with failure of outpatient discharge. Several studies have
suggested that preoperative anemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000019
6/20

heart failure, and uncontrolled or undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnea should be
considered contraindications for outpatient total joint arthroplasty. Specifically,
preoperative anemia (hemoglobin level, <11 g/dL) should be evaluated and strongly
considered in selecting patients for outpatient total joint arthroplasty because patients
who are planned for discharge on the same day of surgery would require inpatient
hospitalization to receive a transfusion if necessary.
Another important aspect in selecting patients for outpatient total joint arthroplasty is
social factors that may affect a patient’s ability to be discharged on an outpatient basis.
Factors such as having a dependent functional status, living alone, having more than
three flights of stairs, or having primary caretaker responsibilities for another person are
risk factors for not being discharged home on the day of surgery.17
Patient Education
Preoperative patient education is critical to safe early discharge.
Because patients are not in the hospital for several days postoperatively, home and physical
therapy education must be provided to the patient and the support team preoperatively.

Patient Education
Patient education is a critical aspect of successful same-day discharge after total joint
arthroplasty. Traditional hospital stays allowed for multiple opportunities to educate
patients about their recovery postoperatively, whereas patients who are discharged on
the same day as surgery must be given such information and education preoperatively
so they are appropriately prepared for their recovery. This also is the reason modern
total joint arthroplasty is associated with a substantially greater amount of preoperative
time spent with the patient, as demonstrated by Kreuger et al.18
Preoperative education can be achieved via several methods and performed by different
members of the care team. Nurses, physical therapists, physician extenders, and
anesthesiologists should be involved in preoperative education for outpatient total joint
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000019
7/20

arthroplasty patients. Live classes, one-on-one meetings, webinars, videos, physical
training sessions, and digital patient engagement platforms all have a role in ensuring
that patients receive the education necessary for safe same-day discharge. Additional
details on this system are found in Video 2.
Video 2 Kim RH: The protocols and pathways that make it work, from Sah AP, mod:
Outpatient joint replacement: Practical guidelines for your program based on evidence,
success, and failure. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Preoperative Pathway
The three key ingredients to a preoperative pathway for outpatient joint replacement are
avoidance of lightheadedness and dizziness, avoidance of nausea and vomiting, and early
intervention for pain control.
The most common reasons for failure to achieve discharge goals on the day of surgery are
lightheadedness, dizziness, and nausea.

Preoperative Pathway
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000019
8/20

Successful outpatient joint replacement programs have carefully designed preoperative
pathways to help decrease the risk of patients being unable to be discharged on the
same day of surgery. Often, studies have noted that failure to be discharged on the day
of surgery most often is related to dizziness, lightheadedness, and nausea; therefore,
careful planning to avoid these occurrences are vital to predictable same-day
discharge.19
Avoidance of dizziness and lightheadedness is best achieved via a preoperative,
intraoperative, and postoperative protocol for hydration. Although historical dogma in
surgery often called for patients to take nothing by mouth after midnight, this actually
dehydrates patients at a time at which they need to be as close to volume neutral as
possible so they can safely undergo surgery and begin ambulating as quickly as possible.
This has led to the current American Society of Regional Anesthesia guidelines, which call
for patients to avoid clear liquids (including water, sports drinks, and other clear liquids)
for 2 hours before a procedure being performed under general anesthesia, regional
anesthesia, or sedation.20
Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a risk factor for failure to participate in
physical therapy and achieve goals for same-day discharge. Commonly, postoperative
nausea is related to dehydration; pain; anesthesia; and the use of intraoperative
medications associated with nausea, such as narcotics. Several methods are available to
attempt to reduce or avoid PONV. A strong program to avoid dehydration is the first
step. The use of preoperative aprepitant, which has been shown to reduce the incidence
of PONV after THA and TKA via a single dose, has been advocated by Parvataneni et al.21
In this prospective randomized study, patients undergoing THA or TKA were randomized
to a study group receiving periarticular injections or a control group receiving patient-
controlled analgesia with or without a femoral nerve block (TKA patients). All patients
received a comprehensive multimodal perioperative protocol. Pain, recovery of
functional milestones, and overall satisfaction were assessed. The THA study group had
substantially lower mean pain scores and higher overall satisfaction than the control
group. No considerable difference in pain scores was observed between the study and
control groups in the TKA cohort. Both study groups had lower narcotic use and adverse
effects and improved early functional recovery. Periarticular injection with a multimodal
protocol was shown to safely provide excellent pain control and functional recovery and

can be substituted for conventional pain control modalities.21 Some studies also have
recommended the use of transdermal scopolamine, placed preoperatively, in select
patients to prevent PONV; however, risk factors for adverse effects, such as dizziness
and somnolence, should be considered.22 In addition, the routine use of antiemetic
agents, such as ondansetron, intraoperatively or postoperatively also has been
advocated. Intraoperative and postoperative corticosteroids also have been shown to
decrease PONV and should be considered in most patients without a medical
contraindication.23 Finally, the avoidance of intrathecal narcotics should be considered
to avoid the PONV associated with their use.24
Preoperative multimodal analgesia also should be a considered in outpatient total joint
arthroplasty programs. Some type of preoperative analgesia is important for a
comprehensive outpatient program. The preoperative pathways are summarized in
Table 2.

Meloxicam: 15 mg if sulfa allergy
Acetaminophen: 1,000 mg
Regional nerve block for total knee arthroplasty

Intraoperative Patient Management
Pain Management
Pain management for outpatient total joint replacement should involve a strong multimodal
pain program, appropriate use of local anesthetic agents, and avoidance of parenteral
narcotics if possible.
Nerve blocks and periarticular injections are very helpful pain adjuncts in total joint
arthroplasty.

Pain Management
A strong multimodal pain management program is essential to the success of outpatient
arthroplasty. The concept of multimodal analgesia was introduced in the early 1990s and
focuses on multiple pathways of analgesia in combination to provide adequate pain
relief without dose-dependent adverse effects of any particular class of medications.25 In
total joint arthroplasty, multimodal pain management usually includes some form of
preoperative analgesia, appropriate anesthetic techniques and intraoperative analgesia,
and postoperative multimodal analgesia with a focus on avoiding parenteral narcotics
because of their substantial adverse effects.
Preoperative analgesia often includes acetaminophen; a NSAID; and, in certain patients,
an oral opioid. Multiple attempts have been made to add other classes of medications to
these preoperative regimens, most commonly gabapentinoids; however, the data do not
appear to support any benefit from their routine use, and some concern exists for
increased cardiopulmonary complications with their use.26,27
Intraoperative anesthesia can be accomplished via neuraxial anesthesia, general
anesthesia, or a combination. From an analgesic perspective, ketamine, intravenous
acetaminophen, intravenous corticosteroids, and ketorolac have been described as
potential components of a multimodal analgesia program.
Another important aspect of intraoperative and postoperative multimodal analgesia,
especially for TKA, is regional and local anesthesia. This can be accomplished via
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Outpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000019
11/20

peripheral nerve blocks, such as adductor canal blocks and interspace between the
popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee blocks and via periarticular injections. The
adductor canal block is a motor-sparing block of the saphenous nerve and the anterior
femoral cutaneous nerve. It is an ultrasonography-guided block that has been shown to
be as effective as a femoral nerve block without the motor weakness concerns
associated with a femoral nerve block.28 However, a adductor canal block may be
technique dependent and a motor block may occur if not performed accurately or if too
much anesthetic agent infiltrates the adductor musculature. Therefore, care should be
taken to ensure that quadriceps function is intact before allowing the patient to
ambulate. The interspace between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee block
is an ultrasonography-guided block of the posterior capsular nerves to provide motor-
sparing analgesia to the back of the knee. It commonly blocks the articular branches of
the tibial nerve, the posterior branches of the obturator nerve, and the posterior
genicular nerves. The addition of the interspace between the popliteal artery and the
capsule of the knee block to an adductor canal block has been shown to be superior for
immediate postoperative pain relief compared with an adductor canal block alone.29 The
final component of intraoperative local injection therapy for total joints is a periarticular
injection. This involves the local infiltration of several possible combinations of
medications in and around the surgical field. Most commonly, these injections include a
local anesthetic with epinephrine, normal saline, and some other adjuvants. Options for
these adjuvants include corticosteroids, clonidine, antibiotic agents, and ketorolac.21
Postoperative multimodal pain regimens are mainly focused on staying ahead of the
pain and avoiding parenteral narcotics because of their associated adverse effects.
These regimens often include acetaminophen, NSAIDS, corticosteroids, and an as-
needed oral narcotic. The use of multimodal analgesia has been associated with
improved outcomes for patients and a decrease in the overall cost of care.30 Additional
details on this system are found in Video 3.

Blood Management
Blood management is integral to early discharge after total joint replacement.

Blood Management
A modern blood management program, including aggressive screening and
management of preoperative anemia and the judicious use of tranexamic acid, is
paramount to the success of an outpatient joint replacement program.
Fluid Management
Fluid management is the key to avoiding lightheadedness and dizziness.

This is achieved via a comprehensive fluid management program that includes encouraging
clear liquid intake until 2 hours before surgery, intraoperative euvolemia, and aggressive
postoperative hydration.

Fluid Management
Fluid management is among the most critical factors associated with the success of
same-day discharge joint replacement. This involves implementation of current
American Society of Regional Anesthesia guidelines, including instructing patients to
continue to drink clear liquids until 2 hours before surgery to avoid dehydration
preoperatively. In addition, keeping patients relatively euvolemic intraoperatively may be
helpful. Finally, aggressive postoperative hydration is essential. Most outpatient joint
arthroplasty programs achieve this via a 500- to 1,000-mL bolus administered to all
patients after they void and by encouraging liquid intake as tolerated. Intraoperative
pathways are summarized in Table 3.

Periarticular injection
Nausea/vomiting

Ondansetron: 4 mg

Postoperative Management
Day of Surgery Management
All patients should be monitored for postoperative urinary retention.
A standardized therapy protocol for the assurance of safe same-day discharge also should be
established.

Day of Surgery Management
Aside from pain management and fluid management, another important aspect of
patient care on the day of surgery is monitoring for perioperative complications that may
delay or inhibit same-day discharge. Outside of lightheadedness, nausea, and vomiting, a
major factor that may prevent same-day discharge is postoperative urinary retention. All
patients should be screened for a history of postoperative urinary retention
Preoperative urology consultation should be considered in patients with such a history.
Risk factors include male sex, administration of more than 1,350 mL of fluid, and the use
of an indwelling urinary catheter.31 Therefore, routine use of Foley catheters should be
avoided if possible. A predictive nomogram also was developed and published in 2020.32
A discharge protocol should be established to determine whether a patient is safe for
same-day discharge after total joint arthroplasty. These criteria often are similar to
requirements for home discharge regardless of the time the patient spends in the
hospital. Most commonly, these discharge requirements include the ability to get into
and out of bed; some required length of independent ambulation; and, if appropriate,
the ability to ascend and descend stairs safely. If patients who can tolerate oral intake,
use appropriate assistive devices, have pain that is well controlled, and can achieve
these activity milestones are safe to be discharged home. The postoperative pathways
are summarized in Table 4.

Postdischarge Management
Postdischarge management does not differ substantially for inpatient or outpatient joint
replacement.
In-person or virtual physical therapy combined with active communication are applicable in
most patients.

Postdischarge Management
Similar to all other patients who undergo joint arthroplasty, patients who undergo
outpatient joint arthroplasty require an appropriate postdischarge plan for follow-up.
Many hospitals or ambulatory surgery centers at which the procedure was performed

will have a protocol for contacting patients the next day to ensure they are safe and that
any home care needs have been addressed. After returning home, patients who have
gone outpatient arthroplasty are no different than patients who have undergone
traditional arthroplasty and have been discharged home. Often, some form of physical
therapy is performed, occasionally with a visiting physical therapist or, more commonly,
via a telehealth or virtual physical therapy program. Mobile, app-based patient
engagement platforms are another option for any arthroplasty patients to continue
exercises and therapy at home.
